title: Somerset
summary: Somerset was laid out in 1801 as the seat of Pulaski County, created in 1799 from Lincoln and Green, on forty acres donated by William Dodson.
bodyMarkdown:
Somerset began with a new county and a good spring. On December 10, 1798, the Kentucky General Assembly created Pulaski County from parts of Lincoln and Green counties, according to [Grokipedia's article on Pulaski County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky). County government began in June 1799. The new county needed a seat, and Somerset was laid out to be it.

## A county named for a Polish general

Pulaski was Kentucky's 27th county. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker for the Town Spring](https://history.ky.gov/markers/town-spring) says it was named for Count Casimir Pulaski, a Polish soldier who came to America to join the Revolution. He served as a brigadier general and died of wounds on October 11, 1779. The marker notes that counties in seven states carry his name.

The land had a longer history. Grokipedia notes a continuing Native American presence in neighboring territories into the early 1800s. Cherokee claims in the country south of the Cumberland were given up in 1805, as told in the story of the [Tellico cession](/stories/tellico-cession-1805-south-of-the-cumberland/).

## Forty acres and a spring

The [KHS marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/town-spring) says Somerset was established as the county seat in 1801 on 40 acres given by William Dodson. [Grokipedia's Somerset article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Somerset,_Kentucky) adds that the site was chosen in 1799 for its central location and its reliable spring.

The path to that spring became the town's most traveled street. The marker records a popular saying: "Whoever drinks from the Old Town Spring will have wisdom and will always return to Somerset."

The name came from the East. The [Wikipedia article on Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset,_Kentucky) says the area was first settled in 1798 by Thomas Hansford. It takes its name from Somerset County, New Jersey, where some early settlers had lived. Somerset was incorporated as a city in 1887.

## War, rails and a lake

In January 1862 the Civil War came close. The Battle of Mill Springs was fought at Logan's Crossroads, now Nancy, west of Somerset. Grokipedia calls it the first significant Union victory of the war. The two sources disagree on its distance and direction from town, so this story leaves that out. A smaller battle followed nearby at Dutton's Hill in 1863.

In 1875 the Southern Railway's tracks were completed, and Wikipedia says the town's population and industry grew. In the late 1930s and early 1940s, library service came from the pack horse library program.

The biggest change came with water. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built Wolf Creek Dam on the Cumberland River, and Grokipedia says construction ran from 1941 to 1952. The dam created Lake Cumberland, which brought flood control, hydropower and a tourism economy to Somerset's hinterland.

## Kentucky today

Somerset is the seat and largest city of Pulaski County. The Town Spring marker stands on South Vine Street. Wikipedia says the Mill Springs Battlefield Visitor Center and Museum opened in 2006 (a claim it marks as needing a citation). Lake Cumberland draws visitors to the region. Wikipedia notes that Somerset is near [Cumberland Falls](/stories/cumberland-falls/) and the [Big South Fork](/stories/yahoo-falls-big-south-fork/) area.
